S1 yielded the highest estimated national net benefit, city-specific optimal strategies varied substantially, revealing pronounced spatial heterogeneity. Our modeling results suggest that intervention strategies may yield inconsistent results across exposure reduction, health outcomes, and economic returns, underscoring the need for multidimensional assessment and locally tailored approaches to maximize the co-benefits of indoor air quality interventions. These model-based findings provide a framework for comparing intervention strategies and informing locally tailored indoor air quality management.

title: Assessing the health and economic burden of sick leave associated with long-term fine particulate matter exposure: a 13-year analysis using German health claims data
abstract: Background Ambient fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) is a major environmental health risk, yet its contribution to sick leave and related productivity losses remains insufficiently quantified. We therefore examined the association between PM 2.5 exposure and all-cause sick leave days and estimated the corresponding model-based burden and productivity losses. Methods Using routine health insurance data from AOK Baden-Württemberg for 2010–2022, we fitted generalized additive models with penalised splines to estimate the exposure–response curve between monthly PM 2.5 exposure and all-cause sick leave days. Models were adjusted for long-term trends, seasonality, temperature, sex, the COVID-19 period, NO 2 , vacation days, and lockdown days, and accounted for spatial heterogeneity using a postal-code-based Markov random field. Model-based exposure contrasts were derived from predicted sick leave days at selected PM 2.5 concentrations. Productivity losses were estimated using the human capital approach. Results PM 2.5 showed a positive non-linear association with sick-leave days (p < 0.001). Compared with 5 µg/m 3 , adjusted predicted sick-leave days were 9.56% higher at 10 µg/m 3 (95% CI 9.09–10.00) and 15.00% higher at 20 µg/m 3 (95% CI 14.20–15.80), while little change was observed between 10 and 15 µg/m 3 (+0.04%, 95% CI − 0.30 to 0.38). The overall non-linear association was supported across additional analyses, although its magnitude and precise shape varied with temporal coverage and covariate adjustment. PM 2.5 concentrations above the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m 3 corresponded to 105 model-attributable excess sick-leave days per 1,000 working-age inhabitants per year, equivalent to approximately 5.31 million excess sick-leave days and €1.56 billion in annual productivity losses in Germany. Conclusion Higher PM 2.5 exposure was associated with a relevant model-attributable burden of sickness absence and productivity losses. These findings suggest that ambient PM 2.5 may be an important population-level correlate of work absence, although causal interpretation is limited by the ecological study design and residual confounding.

title: Increased stillbirth risk associated with heatwave exposure in late pregnancy: evidence from a 3.8 million mother-infant birth cohort
abstract: Background Despite growing evidence linking extreme temperature to adverse birth outcomes, the nexus between heatwaves and stillbirth remains unstudied in low- and middle-income settings. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the effects of different heatwave types on stillbirth risk in an Iranian birth cohort. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort analysis using national data from Iran, encompassing 3.84 million singleton birth records across 749 hospitals in 31 provinces (2013–2018). Heatwaves based on mean temperature (MeanT-HW), maximum temperature (daytime heatwave, DHW), minimum temperature (nighttime heatwave, NHW) and day-night compound heatwave (CHW) were defined as combinations of multiple durations (2, 3, and 4 days) and temperature percentile thresholds (P90, P92.5, P95 and P97.5). The cumulative excess heatwave index (CEHWI) was used to assess the cumulative intensity of heat exposure by summing the daily deviations of Tmean above the predefined threshold during heatwave events. Logistic regression models were employed to separately investigate the associations of stillbirth risk with distinct heatwave exposures under multiple gestational exposure windows. Subgroup analyses were performed to identify population-specific susceptibility stratified by maternal characteristics including age, educational level and residence as well as infant gender. Results Among 3.84 million singleton births (maternal age 28.1 ± 5.8 years), 27,778 stillbirths were identified (28.8 ± 6.5 years). We observed consistent evidence for the effects of MeanT-HW and CEHWI on elevated stillbirth risk in late pregnancy, and the estimated odds ranged from 1.013 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.001–1.025) under P92.5_2d to 1.040 (95% CI: 1.011–1.070) under P97.5_4d for each additional MeanT-HW day and from 1.012 (95% CI: 1.000–1.025) under P95_3d to 1.034 (95% CI: 1.001–1.069) under P97.5_4d for each 1-°C increase in CEHWI during the last week before delivery. Moreover, CHW was associated with greater odds of stillbirth than both DHW and NHW. During the last week before delivery, the excess risks per 1-day increase in exposure reached up to 3.4% (95% CI: 0.5%–6.4%) for DHW under P97.5_3d, 4.3% (95% CI: 1.0%–7.8%) for NHW under P97.5_4d, and 14.2% (95% CI: 4.7%–24.6%) for CHW under P97.5_4d. Subgroup analysis suggested a greater heatwave-related estimates among urban residents compared with rural counterparts. Conclusions This birth cohort study suggested that exposure to various heatwave types during the third trimester and 1–2 weeks before delivery was associated with higher stillbirth odds. These findings highlight the critical need to integrate day-night compound heatwave early warning systems into maternal and child health care services for timely intervention

title: Metabolomic signatures and pathways linking maternal PFAS concentrations to gestational age at birth: a meet-in-the-middle and high dimensional mediation analysis
abstract: Background Preterm birth disproportionately affects Black and African American populations. Greater exposure to environmental toxicants driven by environmental racism may contribute to these disparities. We aimed to identify metabolic intermediates linking maternal per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) exposure to gestational age at birth (GA). Methods We analyzed participants from the Atlanta African American Maternal Child Cohort (2014–2018) with maternal serum collected during early pregnancy (8–14 weeks; n = 307) and late pregnancy (24–30 weeks; n = 238). PFAS concentrations were measured using targeted exposure assessment, and untargeted metabolomics was conducted on maternal serum. GA was abstracted from medical records. We applied two complementary mediation frameworks, Meet-in-the-Middle (MITM) and High-dimensional Mediation Analysis (HIMA), to identify metabolites and pathways linking PFAS exposure with GA outcomes. Results Higher maternal concentrations of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) were associated with increased risk of earlier GA. MITM identified 47 candidate metabolites in early pregnancy and 25 in late pregnancy. HIMA identified palmitoleic acid in early pregnancy and cortisol and N-acetyl-D-galactosamine in late pregnancy. Findings across the two approaches highlighted candidate metabolic signals and pathways, including the tricarboxylic acid cycle, bile acid biosynthesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, and purine metabolism. Conclusions Maternal PFAS exposure was associated with metabolic perturbations that may represent putative biological pathways related to gestational age at birth. This study offers new insights into the potential pathways by which maternal PFAS levels shape the maternal metabolome and influence GA using cutting-edge, targeted exposure assessment, untargeted metabolomics technologies, and high-dimensional mediation techniques.
